name: Ladakh
tagline: High desert of passes, gompas and apricots
meta_description: Plan Ladakh with local facts: Leh, Nubra, Turtuk, Pangong, Tso Moriri, Zanskar. Real costs, permits, acclimatisation and saver to signature trips.
summary: Ladakh is a high-altitude desert on the Indus, reached by air to Leh (3,500 m) or by road over Zoji La or the Manali highway. Go June to September for open passes. Rest 48 hours in Leh before you climb higher. A saver trip runs ₹2,000–3,500 a day.
intro: Ladakh sits behind the main Himalayan wall, so the monsoon barely reaches it. Leh gets about 35 mm of rain a year. What you see is bare brown and violet rock, then a sudden green strip of barley, willow and poplar wherever a glacier stream has been led into fields. Every village is an oasis built by irrigation, and every oasis has its gompa on the ridge above it.

For centuries Leh was a stopover on the caravan routes between Tibet, Kashmir and the Tarim Basin. Traders carried salt, grain, pashm wool, indigo, silk yarn and Banaras brocade through its bazaar, and the road north over the Karakoram Pass led to Yarkand. That mixed past still shows: Buddhist villages in the Indus valley, Shia Kargil to the west, and Balti Turtuk on the Shyok, the only part of India where Balti people live.

Most visitors fly into Leh at 3,500 m. That single fact shapes every good itinerary we write. You spend your first two days doing almost nothing, then add height slowly: Hemis and the Indus monasteries, then Khardung La (5,359 m) to Nubra, then Pangong Tso at about 4,250 m or Tso Moriri at 4,522 m. Rush it and the trip is spent with a headache.

We plan Ladakh in three ways. Saver trips use the Leh bus stand, shared taxis and family guesthouses at ₹1,000–2,000 a night with dinner. Comfort trips use a Ladakh Taxi Union car with driver and the better hotels. Signature trips use the region's few true luxury addresses: a restored manor at Nimmu, a cottage retreat in Nubra, a summer camp facing Thiksey Monastery.

story.title: Salt, pashm and the road to Yarkand

chapters.heading: A kingdom founded by a Tibetan prince
chapters.text: Little is known of Ladakh before the end of the 10th century, when Kyide Nyimagon, a grandson of the Tibetan king Langdarma, founded a kingdom here and conquered western Tibet. Shey, 15 km up the Indus from modern Leh, was the early royal seat, and the first great sculptures there are credited to him. Six centuries later the Namgyal kings moved the court to Leh. Sengge Namgyal built Leh Palace around 1600: nine storeys of mud brick and timber, the royal family on top, stables and stores below. When Dogra forces from Jammu took control of Ladakh in the mid-19th century, the family left the palace for Stok, across the river, where their descendants still keep a museum.

chapters.heading: Caravans to Yarkand and Lhasa
chapters.text: Trade routes converged on Leh from all four directions. From the south came grain, indigo and Banaras brocade; from Tibet came salt and pashm, the fine under-wool of Changthang goats; from the Tarim Basin came charas and silk yarn. Summer and winter routes ran north from Leh over the Karakoram Pass towards Yarkand. Nubra lived off this traffic. When a 16th-century Ladakhi king planned to invade the lands beyond the Karakoram, the people of Nubra persuaded him not to, because the Yarkand trade mattered too much to them. The two-humped Bactrian camels that tourists ride at Hunder today are a living echo of that caravan age.

chapters.heading: The translator and the Kashmiri painters
chapters.text: In the late 10th century the lama-king Yeshe-Ö of Guge sent 21 young scholars to study Buddhism in Kashmir. Only two survived the journey and the climate. One was Rinchen Zangpo, later called the Great Translator, who is credited with founding 108 temples across the western Himalaya. He brought Kashmiri artists with him. Most of their work is lost, but at Alchi, on the Indus 60 km west of Leh, the paintings survived inside small, dark temples: royal drinking scenes, textiles patterned like Kashmiri silk, a three-storey Sumtsek whose inscriptions date it to the 12th century. They are among the oldest surviving paintings in Ladakh, a Kashmiri style that no longer exists in Kashmir itself.

chapters.heading: Barley, apricots and pashm
chapters.text: Height decides what Ladakh can grow. Leh, at about 3,500 m, manages one crop a year, mostly naked barley that is roasted and ground into tsampa. Down the Indus at Khalatse, two crops are possible, and by the time Leh sows its fields in late May, Khalatse's barley is already half grown. Lower Ladakh is apricot country, with more than thirty varieties, and in December 2022 the Raktsey Karpo apricot, known for its white seed, became Ladakh's first product with a Geographical Indication tag. Higher still, on the Changthang plateau, Changpa herders raise Changthangi goats whose winter under-coat becomes pashmina. Water, in all three worlds, comes only from snow and glaciers.

highlights.title: Leh old town and palace
highlights.text: Walk up through the mud-brick lanes below Leh Palace, a nine-storey royal house built around 1600, then climb on to Namgyal Tsemo for the view over the Indus. Mornings are best: the light is clean and the lanes are quiet before the cafes on Changspa Road open.

highlights.title: Khardung La to Nubra
highlights.text: The road north from Leh crosses Khardung La at 5,359 m and drops to the Shyok and Nubra rivers, the old caravan valley to Yarkand. Diskit's 14th-century monastery, the Hunder dunes and their Bactrian camels, and orchard villages make two nights here the minimum.

highlights.title: Pangong Tso at first light
highlights.text: A brackish lake 134 km long at about 4,250 m, two thirds of it beyond the Line of Actual Control. Colours shift from grey to turquoise as the sun climbs. Sleep at Spangmik or Merak, not Lukung, for quieter shores, and bring a down jacket even in August.

highlights.title: Alchi's painted temples
highlights.text: Small dark rooms with some of the oldest surviving paintings in Ladakh, made in a Kashmiri style around the 12th century. Bring patience rather than a camera: photography inside is not allowed, and your eyes need two minutes to adjust before the murals appear.

highlights.title: Tso Moriri and the Changpa
highlights.text: A Ramsar wetland at 4,522 m on the Changthang plateau, where Changpa herders graze yaks and pashmina goats and bar-headed geese breed. Korzok is the only permanent village on its shore. Go only after a week in Ladakh; the altitude is serious.

highlights.title: Turtuk, the Balti village
highlights.text: On the Shyok near the Line of Control, Turtuk was under Pakistani control until 1971 and opened to tourists in 2010. It is one of five Balti villages in India: stone houses, apricot orchards, Balti language and a small old royal house.

money_savers: Book Delhi–Leh flights six to eight weeks ahead for June and July; last-minute fares can triple.
Use the Leh bus stand: the bus to Diskit costs around ₹200 against ₹9,700 for a one-day union taxi.
Shared taxi seats to Nubra and Pangong are posted on flyers along Changspa Road and in Main Bazaar; join one instead of hiring a whole car.
Homestays in Turtuk, Spangmik and Korzok include dinner and breakfast, which saves ₹600–800 a day over eating in camp restaurants.
Travel in the first half of September: the passes are still open, but room rates in Leh drop after the August peak.
Carry a refillable bottle; Leh has filtered-water refill points, and you avoid paying for bottled water at every stop while keeping plastic out of the valleys.
getting_there: By air, Leh's Kushok Bakula Rimpochee Airport has daily flights from Delhi (about 1 h 20 min) plus services from Mumbai, Srinagar, Jammu and Chandigarh. Flights land early to beat afternoon winds and run all year. By road there are two classic approaches. From Srinagar the highway crosses Zoji La to Drass, Kargil and Lamayuru: about 434 km, two days with a night in Kargil. From Manali the Leh–Manali Highway runs through the Atal Tunnel, Keylong, Baralacha La and Tanglang La: about 428 km, one very long day or two with a night in Keylong or Jispa. HRTC runs a Delhi–Leh bus via Keylong in season. The road from Srinagar gives your body the gentlest climb; flying in gives none, so plan rest days. Road openings change each year, so check current status before you travel.
permits: Indian citizens no longer need a separate Inner Line Permit. Instead they pay an Environment and Development Fee online (about ₹400 environment fee, ₹20 a day wildlife fee and an optional Red Cross contribution) and carry the printed receipt to Nubra, Turtuk, Pangong, Tso Moriri and Hanle. Foreign nationals need a Protected Area Permit for these areas, applied for through a registered Leh travel agency with passport copies. Leh town, Hemis, Alchi, Lamayuru, Kargil and Zanskar need no permit. Carry photo ID and several photocopies for checkposts. Rules and fees change; check current status before you travel.

months.weather: Leh −14 to −2 °C, dry and clear; Drass far colder
months.summary: Deep winter. Only flights reach Leh, many guesthouses and cafes close, and pipes freeze, so hotels supply hot water in buckets. This is the month for specialists: the Chadar trek on the frozen Zanskar River, snow leopard tracking in the Rumbak valley of Hemis National Park, and empty monasteries where the only other visitors are pilgrims. Pack expedition-grade clothing and plan buffer days for flight cancellations.
months.tip: Book a hotel that confirms working room heating in writing; electric heaters fail when the power cuts.

months.weather: Leh −12 to 2 °C, clear with light snow spells
months.summary: Still winter, still flight-only, but the light is sharp and Leh comes out for Dosmoche, the festival of the scapegoat, at Leh Palace and at Diskit and Likir monasteries. Snow leopard season continues in Hemis National Park, and the Chadar trek usually runs into mid-February when the ice holds. Khardung La stays open most days, so Nubra is possible in a sturdy car.
months.tip: Dosmoche follows the Tibetan calendar; confirm the year's date with the Leh tourist office before booking flights.

months.summary: The awkward month. Winter is ending but nothing is open yet: the highways from Srinagar and Manali are still closed, many hotels reopen only in April, and the Chadar season is over. Snow leopard trips can still run in early March. If you come, base yourself in Leh, keep to the Indus valley monasteries and expect cold rooms. Prices are at their lowest.
months.tip: Ask before you book whether the guesthouse is open; many families run them only from April to October.

months.weather: Leh 0 to 14 °C, sunny days, freezing nights
months.summary: Apricot blossom month in lower Ladakh. From mid-April the orchards of the Sham valley, Alchi, Khalatse, Garkon and the Kargil side turn white and pink, and villages hold small blossom events. The Srinagar–Leh highway via Zoji La often reopens around this time, so the road approach becomes possible. Higher lakes are still frozen and Changthang is bitterly cold.
months.tip: Blossom moves uphill over about three weeks; start low at Khalatse and follow it to Leh.

months.weather: Leh 5 to 20 °C, dry; passes still snowy
months.summary: The season opens. Hotels in Leh reopen, Pangong begins to thaw, and Nubra's orchards are in leaf. The Manali–Leh highway usually opens late May or in June after snow clearance on Baralacha La and Tanglang La, so most arrivals are still by air or from Srinagar. Crowds are light and rates sensible, but some high passes can close after fresh snow.
months.tip: Keep one spare day in your plan for a pass closure after late-May snowfall.

months.summary: Every road is normally open and the monastery festival season begins. Hemis Tsechu, with its masked cham dances, falls in June or July by the Tibetan calendar; in 2026 it is expected on 24–25 June. Indian school holidays fill flights and hotels, and Pangong is at its busiest. Book camps and Leh rooms early, and leave room in your days for acclimatisation.
months.tip: Fly into Leh mid-week; Friday and Saturday flights from Delhi cost most in June.

months.weather: Leh 13 to 27 °C, warm days; brief showers
months.summary: High summer. Apricots ripen in lower Ladakh and Turtuk from July, Zanskar's Pensi La road is fully open, and wildflowers cover the higher pastures. The Manali road can be cut for a day or two by landslides on the Himachal side when monsoon rain reaches Lahaul. Ladakh itself stays mostly dry. It is busy, but the valleys are large enough to find quiet.
months.tip: Buy dried apricots and apricot oil directly from village stalls in Turtuk and the Sham valley, not in Leh's main bazaar.

months.summary: Still peak season and the best month for the high places: Tso Moriri, Zanskar and the Changthang plateau are at their warmest, and bar-headed geese are on the lakes with their young. The long weekend around Independence Day fills every camp at Pangong. Occasional cloudbursts can damage roads, so build in a buffer day. Evenings at the lakes are still near freezing.
months.tip: Avoid Pangong on the 15 August weekend; go to Tso Moriri instead.

months.summary: Our favourite month. The skies are the clearest of the year, barley turns gold and is harvested, and the crowds thin after the first week. The Ladakh Festival in Leh usually brings dance, polo and archery in September. Nights at the lakes drop below freezing and some camps start closing late in the month, so check before you plan Pangong or Tso Moriri.
months.tip: Ask your hotel for a September rate; many Leh hotels move off peak pricing after 10 September.

months.summary: Autumn colour in the poplar and willow groves, empty roads and low prices. The Manali highway can close any time after mid-October once snow settles on the high passes, and camps at Pangong and Tso Moriri pack up. Leh, Nubra and the Indus valley monasteries remain good. Bring warm layers; mornings start below zero.
months.tip: Plan to fly out rather than drive to Manali after mid-October.

months.summary: The season is over. Most tourist businesses shut, the highways close as snow settles, and water pipes start freezing in the second half of the month. It can suit a quiet, cheap visit to Leh and the Indus valley monasteries if you are well prepared for cold, but there is little infrastructure and the lakes are not sensible.
months.tip: Carry cash; some ATMs outside Leh run dry in the off-season.

months.summary: Mid-winter, but Ladakh celebrates. Ladakhi Losar, the new year, falls on the first day of the 11th Tibetan month, which usually lands in December, two months before Tibetan Losar. Houses are cleaned, fires lit on rooftops and families visit each other for days. Visitors are few; Leh hotels that stay open offer low rates, and the flight-only access makes it a slow, cold, local month.
months.tip: Pack thermal inners for sleeping; few guesthouses heat rooms through the night.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Ladakh?
faqs.a: June to September is best: all roads are normally open, the lakes are accessible and monasteries hold their summer festivals. September has the clearest skies and fewer crowds. April brings apricot blossom in lower Ladakh but the high lakes are frozen. January and February are for specialists: the Chadar trek, snow leopard trips and Dosmoche, with flight-only access and temperatures far below zero. Road openings change each year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a permit for Ladakh?
faqs.a: Indian citizens do not need a separate Inner Line Permit now. They pay an Environment and Development Fee online, roughly ₹400 plus ₹20 a day wildlife fee and an optional Red Cross contribution, then carry the printed receipt and photo ID to Nubra, Turtuk, Pangong, Tso Moriri and Hanle. Leh, Hemis, Alchi, Kargil and Zanskar need no permit. Rules and fees have changed several times since 2014, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I avoid altitude sickness in Ladakh?
faqs.a: Plan your first 48 hours in Leh (3,500 m) as rest: short walks, plenty of water, no alcohol, no long drives. Do not cross Khardung La or sleep at Pangong until your third or fourth night. Coming by road from Srinagar gives a gentler climb than flying. Headache, nausea and breathlessness at rest are warning signs; going lower is the main cure. Talk to your doctor before the trip, especially about medication and any heart or lung condition.

faqs.q: How much does a Ladakh trip cost?
faqs.a: A saver trip with buses, shared taxis and guesthouses costs about ₹2,000–3,500 a person a day, so 7 nights runs roughly ₹18,000–25,000 plus flights. A comfort trip with a private union taxi and good hotels is ₹7,000–12,000 a day. A signature trip at the best hotels and camps with a private guide starts around ₹25,000 a day. Delhi–Leh flights add ₹5,000–15,000 each way depending on season and how early you book.

faqs.q: Does my mobile phone work in Ladakh?
faqs.a: Only postpaid connections work; prepaid SIMs issued outside Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh do not roam here. Jio, Airtel and BSNL postpaid work in Leh, Kargil, Diskit and most larger villages. Pangong and Tso Moriri have patchy coverage, often only BSNL or Jio near the main village. Turtuk and Zanskar have limited signal. Download offline maps, and tell family your plan before you leave Leh. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are there ATMs and card payments in Ladakh?
faqs.a: Leh has many ATMs and most hotels, cafes and shops take UPI and cards when the network works. Kargil, Diskit and Padum have ATMs, but they can run out of cash at weekends and in the off-season. Pangong, Tso Moriri, Turtuk and village homestays are mostly cash. Carry enough cash from Leh for three to four days of travel outside town, in small notes.

faqs.q: Is Ladakh safe for solo women travellers?
faqs.a: Ladakh is one of the more relaxed regions in India for women travelling alone, and many do. Guesthouse families are used to solo guests, and shared taxis are a normal way to travel. Usual care applies: share your plan, avoid hitching alone late in the day, and pick registered taxis from the union stands. The bigger risks are altitude and remote roads, so do not drive high passes alone and keep a charged phone.

faqs.q: Is Ladakh suitable for children and senior travellers?
faqs.a: Yes, with a slower plan. Children and older travellers acclimatise like anyone else, but may not describe symptoms clearly, so watch for tiredness, poor appetite and headache. Keep to two full rest days in Leh, pick Nubra (about 3,100 m) over overnight stays at the lakes, and use a private car so you can stop. Talk to your doctor before travelling, especially with infants or heart and lung conditions.

faqs.q: Can I drive or ride to Ladakh from Manali or Srinagar?
faqs.a: Yes, both highways are open in summer. Srinagar to Leh is about 434 km over Zoji La, usually broken at Kargil. Manali to Leh is about 428 km via the Atal Tunnel and Tanglang La, usually broken at Keylong or Jispa. The Srinagar side often opens around April–May and Manali in late May or June, both closing with winter snow. Self-drive vehicles are fine, but local rules restrict outside rental cars and bikes on some routes. Check current status before you travel.
